https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89: A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.
The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.
It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.
The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.

Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland . The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.
Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".
Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X. , external

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
Neither of Libya's rival administrations has formally declared support for either side in the Russia-Ukraine war, but they have contrasting ties with Moscow and Kyiv.
The head of the Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east of the country, has longstanding links with Russia.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq1j: Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r4: The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says , external .
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".
In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".
Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".

Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwx2: The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service

Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.

Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.

The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.

While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
Although the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues, the two leaders did not mention the border dispute in their public remarks

A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.

Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.

His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.

According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq78: Many Nigerian rely on boats to travel beyond their villages (file photo)
Nigerian search and rescue teams are racing against time to find survivors after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
There have been reports that the boat was carrying more than 300 people but the Nema spokesperson said this wasn't correct. He did not say how many people were on board but said it was overcrowded.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.

"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.

In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxyv: Uebert Angel is still in police custody following a dramatic arrest over the weekend
A well-known Zimbabwean preacher has been arrested on indecent assault and sodomy allegations, local police said.

Uebert Angel, who leads an international charismatic church with branches around the world, was arrested during a church service in Harare on Sunday. Pictures and footage of the dramatic arrest have since been circulated online.
In one video, a convoy of vehicles is seen escorting the self-styled prophet as he sits in the back of a police van surrounded by armed police officers.
The controversial founder of Spirit Embassy was also appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large to Europe and the Americas back in 2021 by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

In 2023, he made headlines when an undercover report by Al Jazeera claimed that he had offered to use his diplomatic status to launder large amounts of money through a gold-smuggling scheme in the country.
According to the Qatar-based network, Angel, 48, told reporters working undercover that the scheme was approved by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Zimbabwean police only released a brief statement confirming his arrest but a member of his team told reporters the British Zimbabwean national was still in police custody and it was unclear when he'd make an appearance in court.

"It can be in the afternoon or tomorrow [Tuesday]. We are still within the legal framework [for him to appear in court]," Professor Lovemore Madhuku told state-owned broadcaster ZBC in a clip posted online.
This is not the first time the prominent preacher has been accused of improper behaviour.

A report by local online publication ZimLIVE in 2021 said that Angel had previously faced allegations of sexual impropriety from several women, at least five of whom are in England. The charismatic preacher has denied the allegations, the outlet added at the time.
Angel's church has branches in Zimbabwe, South Africa and the UK and he known for his ties to other African preachers like Malawian televangelist Shepherd Bushiri.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr93: Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney

Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster , external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's , external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media. , external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwdr: A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.

Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march

One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.

"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5rm: Extra forces have been deployed to guard the facility where 'Chapo Isidro' is in custody
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.
The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.
In a statement published on social media , external , the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.
It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.
The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.
It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".
Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital
Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.
They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.
Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued, in which four soldiers and 16 "members of organised crime" were killed, according to the latest figure released by the defence minister on Monday.
Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.
As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.
There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.
US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".
The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.
He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.
As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".
It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.
According to think tank Insight Crime , external , Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg: The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila , in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

New Zealand was ready to support a draft deal that prompted UN climate talks to collapse without a decision.
COP31 ended on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, with no consensus after more than two weeks of fraught negotiations.
The final draft deal, known as a cover decision, avoided any mention of the fossil fuels driving global warming.
The European Union, together with Panama and several other countries, formally objected to the draft, saying it was "unconscionable" to support it.
A spokesperson for New Zealand's caretaker climate minister, Simon Watts, said New Zealand was "ready to support a consensus on the cover decision".
Asked to confirm if that meant New Zealand supported the final draft as it stood, the spokesperson said: "Yes - New Zealand would have supported consensus in the room."

Despite the lack of a decision, the conference - which Watts attended for three days last week - was "a valuable opportunity for New Zealand to engage internationally and strengthen important relationships", the spokesperson said.
Green MP Francisco Hernandez, who was at COP31 until this morning NZT, said the EU and others were right to reject the draft decision.
The lack of any language about a transition away from fossil fuels was especially disappointing, he said.

"That was probably the most egregious thing for us - not naming fossil fuel as the thing that's causing climate change is basically like going to a cancer conference and not acknowledging smoking as the cause of lung cancer," he said.
The language about finance to assist vulnerable countries to adapt to climate change was also too weak, he said.
"There were some positive things in the text - things like the electrification target of 35 percent by 2035 - but unfortunately there was no real language there that it had to be clean energy."
The EU and others were right to walk away from the deal, he said.
"The draft text was just so weak - it doesn't meet the moment."
There were rumours all weekend that the deal would not pass, and a "febrile" atmosphere among the negotiating teams.
The failure to agree in a cover decision did not mean COP31 itself had failed, he said.
"I think people would be remiss to come away ... with the impression that we need to do less on climate, not more... This COP failed because it wasn't ambitious enough."
However, there was "probably merit" in considering whether the format of climate COPs - particularly the requirement for consensus decision-making - needed a second look.

"It really doesn't make sense to allow a small group of fossil fuel producers to hold the rest of the world hostage... Saudi Arabia was quite aggressive in trying to block progress on any of the texts."
Otago University climate and energy researcher Sebastian Gehricke said he had paid less attention to the annual talks in recent years because of how frustrating he found them.
"The word 'fossil fuels' in itself has been a hot topic, and that seems farcical to me because that's the whole point - the key driver of mitigating climate change is to reduce use of fossil fuels."
Even when the talks did result in deals or goals being set, there was a lack of follow-through.
"You look at the climate finance pledge, where developed nations promised to provide financing for climate projects for adaptation and mitigation of US$100 billion per year, and that was never hit.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.

"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.
Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.
Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

The high street retailer said there was no evidence that customers' personal data had been compromised.

The firm - which has its headquarters in Enderby, Leicestershire - said it had been informed by one of its suppliers about the incident, which led to "unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next".
"We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier," the company told investors.
"Our investigations are ongoing. However, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.
"The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next."
The company added it was treating the situation "with the utmost seriousness", and working with the supplier as well as the police and regulators.
Next is the latest retailer to be caught up in a cyber breach.
In October, Asos said an "unauthorised party" had gained access to an employee's account , leading customers to receive a phone alert saying that the retailer had been hacked.
The firm said the attacker gained access to some personal data, including names and contact details belonging to customers.
In 2025 Marks & Spencer suffered from a major cyber-attack, which forced it to stop all online sales for about six weeks and led to some empty shelves in shops.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7: Catering giant Compass Group is planning to switch its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US in a move which will deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange.
A source close to the company told the BBC an official announcement was expected to be made in its full-year results on Tuesday.
Compass Group is made up of several brands which supply food and drink to various places, ranging from football stadiums and visitor attractions to schools, universities and large corporations.

It is understood the proposed shift to the US, which was first reported by the Financial Times , external , is being made due to the number of investors and the increasing business Compass has across the Atlantic.
North America accounts for two-thirds of its business, which drove its total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn.
However, such a move would deal a further blow to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), which has seen a growing number of firms leave the UK to list shares in the US in recent years.
These include tech firm Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter.
Long-running speculation also remains over the future of London stalwarts Shell and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

Compass describes itself as "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of" due to its plethora of catering and hospitality brands it operates its business under, which include Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells.
'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

The company was created during the Second World War after the Factories Canteen Order meant large manufacturing or munitions firms employing 250 people or more had an obligation to provide hot meals for workers.
Today, Compass operates across more than 25 countries and employs more than 600,000 people.

It is understood the group's proposed move to the US will have no impact on the number of UK employees and a consultation process with investors could take more than a year. It is expected to retain a secondary listing in London.
In a sign its listing could change, Compass changed the currency in which it trades its standard shares on the LSE from sterling to US dollars in April this year.
The boss of the LSE recently called on the government to do more to back homegrown companies and make the UK "more attractive" to invest in the domestic stock market.

Dame Julia Hoggett told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so.
Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crm4: Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills
Energy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.
Energy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.
So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.
With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.
turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently
turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use
turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum
These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.
Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.
Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.
Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.
Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.
The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.
Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available , not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.
There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes .
This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.
Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.
Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment , external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.
Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme , external can help you repay energy debt.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g: The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.
Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."
She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."
However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.
It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.
Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.
Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.
As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid , although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.
A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.
Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.
Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly: The disability minister has been looking into disability benefits for a year for his review, which is to be published on Tuesday

A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.
Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".
Writing in the Times , external , he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".
It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.
He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".
"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.
"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."
He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform, which attempted to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.
More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.
The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.
Disability benefit not fit for purpose, minister leading review says
Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
Sir Stephen's long-awaited review comes only a week after a former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn handed down his proposed reforms to tackle youth unemployment .
The government welcomed the Milburn review, which included a recommendation to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".
At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.
No 10 has said the government would consider the Timms review "alongside Milburn's and respond in the coming weeks".

Downing Street has not ruled out the possibility that some people who currently receive Pip could have a reduced entitlement in the future and would not say if the review's recommendations would lead to a reduced welfare bill.

The cost of Pip is expected to rise to more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020. It was being claimed by 4m people in the UK as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9: Thousands of customers were affected by supply disruptions during high temperatures in May
South East Water has reported a half-year loss after penalties and £29m of costs following disruption to water supplies over the summer.

The company, which serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England, recorded a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September, compared with a profit of £18.2m during the same period last year.
In July, regulator Ofwat ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after supply interruptions hit customers across Kent and Sussex which affected more than 286,000 customers.
The company spent £29m responding to further supply interruptions during summer heatwaves in Kent and Sussex .
This included providing bottled water, setting up emergency water stations and compensating customers.
South East Water said it had set aside £14.6m in its latest financial results to cover the redress package.
The company supplies water to customers in Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.
Hosepipe bans remain in force across all areas supplied by South East Water.
In October, it was forced to ask shareholders for £50m after warning earlier in the year that it required additional funding in order to stay afloat.
The company said there were "early signs of improvement" following changes to its leadership team and plans for a "significant transformation" of the business.
Earlier this year, John Halsall was appointed chief executive after former chief executive David Hinton and chair Chris Train stepped down .
The departures followed criticism from MPs who said they had "no confidence" in the company's leadership after a review of repeated supply outages.
Richard Morse is due to become chair of the company on 3 December, succeeding interim chair Lisa Clement.
South East Water said the initial signs were "encouraging", although it warned improvements would take time to become fully visible to customers.
A spokesperson for the company said: "We know that customers will not judge us on the number of initiatives we launch or the promises we make.

"They will judge us on whether their water supply is more reliable, whether we communicate better and whether we provide the right support when they need it – we look forward to providing the evidence in future results."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d: Ffion, Yugraj and Jessica say being ghosted has become a common part of applying for jobs
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?
So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.
It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".
The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.
But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?
Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.
But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".
He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."
Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.
The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.
Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.
"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.
Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report , external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.
"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.
Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.
And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.
But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.
Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.
"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.
The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.
But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?
Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr: The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.
Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.
The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with bills, but one Citizens Advice adviser said it was a "drop in the ocean" while a pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.
"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".
The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.
Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.

The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.
The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget .
The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.
But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.
One Citizens Advice adviser said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.
"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."
The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.
"Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said.
"Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."
Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.
When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.
